meta.title: AQ Learning
meta.subtitle: lecture playlists, watch progress and AI hand-drawn notes - the whole system

cover.summary: Three small programs: a vanilla-JS UI, a Node + SQLite app backend and a Python AI worker. Every file, data store and request, mapped end to end.
cover.big_idea: Node owns state, Python owns the slow AI work!

sections.title: architecture, the 30,000ft map
sections.subtitle: three programs, one job each

blocks.text: AQ Learning turns YouTube lectures into playlists you can watch in order, with resume-where-you-left-off progress and hand-drawn study notes. It is **three small programs**, not one big one, and each has exactly one job.

items: **lecture-notes-ui** - vanilla JS single page: playlists, player, progress bars, notes viewer. No build step.
**aq-api** (Node + Express + SQLite, :5180) - the application backend: users, playlists, videos, watch progress, notes records cached by video_id. Serves the UI too.
**lecture-notes-ai** (Python + Flask, :5055) - the AI/media worker: YouTube transcript, LLM notes, PDF. Knows nothing about users.

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: Node owns state and identity, Python owns slow, expensive, stateless work. The UI only ever talks to one door (:5180); Node calls Python on 127.0.0.1.

diagram.title: the big picture
diagram.caption: browser -> Node (state) -> Python (AI) -> the internet

key_takeaways: Three programs, one job each: UI shows, Node remembers, Python generates.
The UI has one front door (:5180); Python is an internal worker on localhost.
Node is the place future auth (OAuth) plugs in, so Python never needs users.

recall.q: Walk me through the architecture in one breath.
recall.a: Browser UI -> aq-api (Express, auth middleware, SQLite for playlists/progress/notes records) -> for new notes it calls the Python worker, which fetches the transcript from YouTube, has an LLM write notes, validates them and renders HTML/PDF.

sections.title: tech stack
sections.subtitle: boring tools on purpose

rows: vanilla JS + CSS, IIFE modules on `window.AQ`
no build, no npm; opens anywhere
one file DB, zero native deps
Gemini, Groq, xAI Grok, Hugging Face via plain `requests`
Rough.js, bundled fonts (Kalam, Patrick Hand, Caveat)

blocks.text: Pattern: every dependency earns its place. The Python engine uses `requests` directly instead of five vendor SDKs, and the UI avoids a framework so it needs no toolchain.

diagram.title: the stack, top to bottom
diagram.caption: each layer only talks to the one below

key_takeaways: No framework on the UI, no SDKs in the worker, no native DB driver in Node.
Python is the only place that needs pip packages; Node needs just Express.
Edge or Chrome is only needed to print PDFs; HTML and JSON work without it.

recall.q: Why plain `requests` instead of each provider's SDK?
recall.a: Four providers means four SDKs to install and keep compatible. One small `_Client` speaks the OpenAI-style or Gemini JSON over HTTP, handles retries and key scrubbing in one place, and adding a provider is a table entry.

sections.title: repo layout
sections.subtitle: one workspace, three apps + docs

blocks.text: Everything lives under `D:\AQspace`. The three apps are siblings with no shared code; they only share an HTTP contract. Two old folders are leftovers.

blocks.code:
D:\AQspace
  lecture-notes-ui\   UI: index.html + 13 .js + styles.css (no build)
  aq-api\             Node app backend: src/ sql/ test/ data/aq.db
  lecture-notes-ai\   Python worker

  docs\               this notebook + ARCHITECTURE.md
  backend\ frontend\  empty Vite/Express scaffolds (unused)

blocks.text: `D:\AQspace\backend` (port 3005 hello-world) and `D:\AQspace\frontend` (React + Vite template) are unrelated scaffolds, not part of the running system.

diagram.title: repo tree
diagram.caption: what each folder is for

key_takeaways: lecture-notes-ui, aq-api and lecture-notes-ai are independent siblings.
notes_engine is a pip-installable package: CLI, library and web all use it.
Only an HTTP contract connects the apps, so each can be replaced alone.

recall.q: Why keep the UI, API and worker in separate folders?
recall.a: Different runtimes and different change rates: UI is static files, Node is stateful, Python is heavy and stateless. The seams are HTTP contracts, so any one can be swapped or deployed separately.

sections.title: data layer
sections.subtitle: where each byte lives

blocks.text: State is split by **who owns it**. Users' playlists and progress belong in the app database; generated files belong in the worker's job folders; the browser keeps only caches.

rows: users, videos, playlists, playlist_videos, watch_progress, notes_jobs
"1" = local edits not yet sent to aq-api

blocks.text: The old standalone page also stores `lna.key.<provider>` and `lna.provider` (API key, only if you tick Remember). Keys are never written to disk server-side.

diagram.title: browser copy vs app database
diagram.caption: the UI-side cache and the Node source of truth

key_takeaways: Playlists and progress are durable data: they live in SQLite behind Node.
Python holds only temporary job state and files; a restart loses job ids.
The notes record cached by video_id means two users never pay twice for one video.

recall.q: Why cache notes by video_id in Node when Python already writes files?
recall.a: Python's files are temporary (24h) and its job ids die on restart. A Node record keyed by the 11-char video id survives, so a video is generated once and every playlist, user and device reuses it.

sections.title: request flow: get notes
sections.subtitle: click to PDF, end to end

blocks.text: The slowest path in the system. The UI never waits on one long request: it starts a job and **polls**.

items: UI sends `POST /api/v1/notes/<videoId>` to aq-api (video must be in one of the user's playlists).
Node checks `notes_jobs` for a live record of that video_id; done or running is returned at once (200), nothing new starts.
On a miss Node calls Python `POST /api/jobs` {url, provider}, gets a job_id and inserts a queued record (202).
Python thread: transcript (0-25%), LLM notes (25-85%), HTML+PDF (85-100%).
UI polls `GET /api/v1/notes/<videoId>` about every 1.5 s; Node refreshes from Python `GET /api/jobs/<id>` at most every 0.8 s.
On done Node marks the record done; the UI frames `/notes/<videoId>/html`, which Node streams from Python.

blocks.text: Max 2 jobs run at once on the server; the UI queues extra videos client-side. When `AQ.api.available()` is false the UI falls back to calling Python on :5055 directly.

diagram.title: notes generation
diagram.caption: polling, not waiting

key_takeaways: The UI polls; it never holds a request open for minutes.
Progress is stage-mapped: transcript 0-25, notes 25-85, render 85-100.
A cache hit short-circuits everything after step 2.

recall.q: Why a job + polling instead of one long HTTP request?
recall.a: Notes take seconds to minutes (long lectures need many LLM calls). Proxies and browsers time out long requests; a job returns 202 immediately and exposes stage and percent for a progress bar.

sections.title: watch & resume flow
sections.subtitle: the player remembers where you stopped

blocks.text: `player.js` embeds a `youtube-nocookie.com` iframe and loads the YouTube IFrame API once. A 1-second timer reads the **real** playback position and hands it to the store.

items: Open a video: `AQ.store.watchInfo(id)` gives pos/dur; start > 0 shows "Resumed at m:ss".
Every second `tick()` calls `S.watchSave(id, {pos, dur})`; storage writes are silent.
At >= 95% of the duration, or on the ended event, `done` becomes true.
Replaying a finished video and stopping early flips it back to Resume.
On dialog close `S.notify()` re-renders cards and rows (bars, labels); `api.js` sends the record to aq-api (debounced 2 s).
`learnDuration()` fills a missing duration from the real player.

blocks.text: Rows get their button text from `watchLabel`: Play, Resume * 12:34, or Replay. The `storage` event keeps other tabs in sync.

diagram.title: watch state loop
diagram.caption: from the YouTube iframe to the progress bars

key_takeaways: The position is measured, not guessed: it comes from the player itself.
done = ended event or >= 95% of duration.
Memory is the source of truth; a blocked localStorage never breaks playback.

recall.q: How does resume work, and what if the YouTube API is blocked?
recall.a: A 1 s timer stores {pos, dur} per video id; reopening starts at pos. If the IFrame API cannot load, the plain embed still plays, just without saved progress.

sections.title: notes pipeline in Python
sections.subtitle: URL -> transcript -> notes -> notebook

blocks.text: `notes_engine.generate(url, provider, ...)` is the whole worker in one call; the Flask server runs the same stages with extra status reporting. Progress is remapped to one global 0-100 bar.
The same engine has three front doors: the Flask web server, the CLI `python -m notes_engine URL` and the library import. Exit codes tell a script what failed: 3 transcript, 4 AI provider, 5 no PDF.

diagram.title: engine stages
diagram.caption: each stage can fail with its own user-safe error

key_takeaways: generate() = ingest -> llm -> validate -> render, with one global progress bar.
IngestError, LLMError and PdfError carry messages that are safe to show users.
If only the PDF fails, HTML and JSON are still saved and a warning is returned.

recall.q: What happens if the PDF step fails but the notes were written?
recall.a: The job still finishes as done with a warning: notes.json and notes.html are kept and linked, pdf_path is None. Only when both HTML and PDF fail does the job become an error.

sections.title: ingest.py: transcripts
sections.subtitle: three fallbacks, one clean format

blocks.text: `ingest.py` (1,200 lines) turns a link into `{video_id, title, channel, duration_sec, language, source, segments[]}`. It validates the link first, which doubles as the SSRF guard: only 11-char ids from known YouTube hosts get through.

items: `parse_video_id` accepts watch, youtu.be, shorts, embed, live; anything else is rejected.
Metadata: yt-dlp info, falling back to the oEmbed endpoint.
Try 1: youtube-transcript-api, manual captions before auto, English first.
Try 2: yt-dlp subtitle download (json3 or vtt).
Try 3 (only with a Groq key): download audio, ffmpeg 16 kHz mono in 10-minute chunks, Groq Whisper.
Clean: strip sound cues, dedupe overlapping cues, merge into sentences.
`chunk_transcript` slices text for the LLM (12,000 chars, 400 overlap) with a `[mm:ss]` marker every 30 s.
`get_playlist` lists up to 200 videos via yt-dlp, skipping private/deleted ones.

diagram.title: fallback chain
diagram.caption: stop at the first method that works

key_takeaways: Order: captions API, yt-dlp subtitles, then Whisper only if a Groq key exists.
Private, live and unavailable videos stop the chain early with a clear message.
Cleaning and 30 s time markers let the LLM stamp sections with timestamps.

recall.q: Why validate the URL so strictly before any network call?
recall.a: The server fetches whatever it is given, so an unchecked URL could point it at internal addresses (SSRF). Only an 11-char id from allowed YouTube hosts passes, and the player URL is rebuilt from that id.

sections.title: llm.py & prompts.py
sections.subtitle: single pass vs map-reduce

blocks.text: `llm.generate_notes` picks a strategy from transcript size and the provider's limits (`_profile`). `prompts.py` holds the rules (knowledge only, faithful, 2-4 takeaways, one recall question per section) and four message builders.

items: Target size: about one section per 2.5 minutes, clamped to 6-18.
A `_Pacer` keeps the trailing minute under ~85% of the token limit; 429s sleep for Retry-After.
Up to 5 attempts per call; bad JSON is repaired (`fix_json_messages`) or salvaged if truncated.
The key only goes in a header and is scrubbed from every error message.

diagram.title: two strategies
diagram.caption: short lectures get one call, long ones are map-reduced

key_takeaways: Short lecture: one call. Long lecture: digest each slice, compose batches, write cover/glossary/recap.
Single pass that returns too few sections falls back to map-reduce.
Rate limits are handled by pacing before sending, not only retrying after 429.

recall.q: How do you handle a lecture longer than the model's context or rate limit?
recall.a: Map-reduce: chunk the transcript, make a compact digest per chunk, pack digests into batches that each compose 2-10 sections, then one small call writes subtitle, glossary and recap. A pacer and retries keep each call inside the provider's token-per-minute budget.

sections.title: notes_schema.py: contract
sections.subtitle: forgiving in, strict out

blocks.text: LLM output is messy, so `validate_notes` **coerces instead of rejecting**. It raises only when no section survives. Its output is the single contract between prompts, renderer and UI (`docs/notes-schema.md`).

items: Section numbers are always rebuilt as 2, 3, 4... (page 1 is the cover).
`cover.toc` and every `next` footer are regenerated from the final list, so they cannot drift.
Facts (title, channel, duration, url, language) come from the transcript, not the model.
Caps: 24 sections, 14 blocks, 8 diagram nodes (mindmap 10), labels 40 chars, 30 glossary terms.
Aliases are mapped: `flowchart` -> flow, `mind map` -> mindmap, `children` lists -> `parent` ids.

blocks.text: `validate_notes(validate_notes(x))` is stable: running it twice changes nothing. That is what makes it safe to re-validate stored notes.

diagram.title: the Notes JSON
diagram.caption: everything the renderer needs

key_takeaways: validate_notes coerces: it only fails when there is nothing usable.
Derived fields (toc, next, numbers) are rebuilt, never trusted from the model.
9 block types and 8 diagram types are the whole vocabulary.

recall.q: Why coerce LLM JSON instead of rejecting bad output?
recall.a: Retrying costs tokens and time, and models are nearly right most of the time. Clamping lengths, fixing aliases and rebuilding derived fields rescues almost every answer deterministically, with no extra API calls.

sections.title: pdf.py: the notebook
sections.subtitle: Python lays out, the browser paginates

blocks.text: `render_html` builds one self-contained page: fonts inlined as base64, SVG diagrams laid out **in Python** (text measured with the bundled fonts via PyMuPDF so labels never overflow), then the browser script paginates and sketches.

items: Escape all text (`html.escape`); re-allow only **bold** and `code`.
Diagram builders (`_svg_flow`, `_svg_stack`, ..., `_svg_sequence`) emit SVG with plain strokes + seeded shape specs.
`templates/notebook.js` pours units into fixed A4 page boxes, splitting lists, tables and code across pages.
Vendored `rough.js` redraws the shapes hand-drawn; every page gets rings, footer and `pg. N / M`.
`render_pdf` runs headless Edge/Chrome `--print-to-pdf` (retry with a longer virtual-time budget).
`_pdf_ok` reads the PDF back: every page must say `pg. N / M` with M = real page count.

diagram.title: HTML to PDF
diagram.caption: layout in Python, pagination in the browser

key_takeaways: Text is escaped before any markup is added back: notes cannot inject HTML.
Diagrams are measured in Python so nothing overflows; Rough.js only adds the wobble.
A PDF is accepted only when every page's `pg. N / M` matches the page count.

recall.q: How do you know the generated PDF is correct?
recall.a: After printing, PyMuPDF reads every page's footer; the PDF is accepted only if each page says pg. N / M with M equal to the real page count. Otherwise it retries with more render time, then raises PdfError.

sections.title: Flask server: the worker
sections.subtitle: jobs in memory, files on disk

blocks.text: `backend/app/server.py` (650 lines) is an app factory, `create_app()`. Modules `ingest`, `llm`, `pdf` are imported **lazily inside the worker** so the server still starts if one is broken.

rows: status, stage, pct, message, meta, links, warning, error
the three outputs (html allowed in a local iframe)

items: `State` holds the jobs dict, a lock, a 10-per-60 s rate bucket, a separate playlist bucket and 2 playlist slots.
Each job runs in a daemon thread `_run_job`; max 2 active, otherwise 429.
`cleanup_old_jobs` deletes job folders older than 24 h at startup.

diagram.title: server anatomy
diagram.caption: request guard, then routes, then a job thread

key_takeaways: Lazy imports keep the server alive even with a broken module.
Concurrency is bounded: 2 active jobs, 10 new jobs per 60 s, 2 playlist fetches.
Job status is in memory (restart = 404); files on disk last 24 hours.

recall.q: Why run jobs in threads with in-memory state instead of a queue?
recall.a: It is a single-user local worker, so a thread plus a dict is the simplest thing that works. The cost: a restart loses job ids, which is why Node caches the finished notes record by video_id.

sections.title: python files, one line each
sections.subtitle: every file in lecture-notes-ai

rows: rules + message builders (digest, compose, final, fix-json)
diagram SVG layout, HTML build, headless PDF
pagination, rings, footer / paper + print styles
Kalam, Patrick Hand, Caveat, JetBrains Mono (OFL)

key_takeaways: notes_engine has no web code; the Flask server is a thin shell around it.
The CLI, the library and the server all call the same generate stages.
Fonts, templates and Rough.js ship inside the package, so PDFs are reproducible.

recall.q: Where would you add a fifth LLM provider?
recall.a: In `llm.PROVIDERS` (label, default model, key hint) and `_ENDPOINTS`, a size profile in `_BASE_PROFILES`, and the env var in `ENV_KEYS`; the server and UI read the provider table, so they pick it up automatically.

sections.title: UI core files
sections.subtitle: shell, data, helpers, screens

blocks.text: No bundler: `index.html` loads plain scripts in dependency order, and every file is an IIFE that hangs its API on one global, `window.AQ`.

rows: shell: top bar, `#view`, modal, script order
tokens + all components, black glass theme
playlist CRUD, sanitising, watch progress, limits
sync adapter: probes aq-api, imports once, writes through, dirty flag
accessible modal: focus trap, Esc, restore focus
hash router, home grid, chroma cards, detail, drag-and-drop

blocks.text: Safety rule across the UI: user text is only set with `textContent`; there is no `innerHTML` anywhere.

diagram.title: script load order
diagram.caption: later files depend on earlier ones

key_takeaways: One global namespace (AQ) and ordered script tags replace a bundler.
store.js has no DOM code; app.js renders from store and re-renders on notify().
Routes: `#/` home, `#/playlist/<id>`, `#/playlist/<id>/notes/<videoId>`.

recall.q: How is the UI organised without a framework or build step?
recall.a: Small IIFE modules sharing one `window.AQ` namespace, loaded in order. `store.js` owns data and emits change events, `app.js` listens, re-renders the active hash route and writes the DOM only through textContent.

sections.title: UI feature modules
sections.subtitle: player, notes, import, effects

rows: youtube-nocookie embed, prev/next, saves position every 1 s
`AQ.notesJobs`: start/poll/retry/urls, max 2 running, resumes after reload
Get notes button: none, running %, ready, retry
notes panel: iframe of notes.html, Download PDF
slide-in notes panel, list shrinks to nav (FLIP animation)
import dialog: fetch playlist, preview, create local copy

diagram.title: window.AQ namespace
diagram.caption: who exposes what

key_takeaways: notesJobs is the shared brain: rows, player and button all read it.
split.js keeps the SAME list node across states, so morphing is a cheap FLIP animation.
All motion respects prefers-reduced-motion.

recall.q: Why does notes.js keep job ids in localStorage?
recall.a: Server job ids are in memory and the page may reload mid-generation. Storing {videoId: {jobId, state}} lets queued or running jobs resume polling, and a 404 from the server turns into "Notes expired, generate again".

sections.title: api.js: the sync adapter
sections.subtitle: local first, server as source of truth

blocks.text: `store.js` stays **synchronous** and keeps `localStorage` as the offline cache. `api.js` (loaded right after it) mirrors everything to aq-api, so the UI never waits on the network and still works if the server is down.

items: Boot: probe `GET /api/v1/health` on the same origin, then on `http://127.0.0.1:5180`.
`reconcile()`: `GET /me`. If not `bootstrapped` (or the dirty flag is set) push local data with `POST /sync/import`; otherwise pull playlists + progress.
`store.applyRemote()` adopts the server's data (a newer local watch record still wins) and re-renders.
Every store change calls `AQ.api.record(name, args)`; writes are queued **in order** (create, PATCH, DELETE, PUT order...).
Watch progress is debounced: one `PUT /progress/<videoId>` per video every 2 s, flushed on tab hide / `pagehide`.
Server unreachable: `aq.dirty.v1 = 1`; on `online` or tab focus the whole local state is pushed again.

blocks.text: Last writer wins by the `updated` timestamp: the server ignores an older progress write than the one it holds.

diagram.title: sync on start
diagram.caption: probe, reconcile, then write-through

key_takeaways: localStorage is the cache, aq-api is the source of truth; the UI code stays synchronous.
Writes go through in order; progress is debounced to one PUT per video per 2 s.
A dirty flag guarantees offline edits are pushed later, never lost.

recall.q: What happens to edits you make while the server is down?
recall.a: They are saved to localStorage immediately and `aq.dirty.v1` is set. When the page regains focus or the browser goes online, api.js reconnects and pushes the whole local state with POST /sync/import in replace mode, then clears the flag.

sections.title: aq-api: the Node backend
sections.subtitle: state, identity and the front door

blocks.text: `aq-api` owns users, playlists, videos, watch progress and one notes record per video_id. It proxies the two slow things (notes, YouTube import) to Python and serves the UI on :5180. One dependency: `express`.

rows: entry + env config (port, DB, Python URL, limits)
`createApp`: middleware order, routers, static UI, JSON errors
node:sqlite + migrations; all SQL scoped by userId
fixed-path client for the Python worker
auth seam (local user today); headers, host guard, CORS, rate limit

items: Routes live under `/api/v1/...`: playlists, progress, notes, import/youtube, sync/import, health, me.
`authenticate` sets `req.user` before every data route; swap it for OAuth via `createApp(config, {authenticate})`.
Node >= 24: SQLite is the built-in `node:sqlite`, no native module to compile.

diagram.title: a request inside aq-api
diagram.caption: guards first, then auth, then the route

key_takeaways: Node owns state and identity; Python stays stateless.
Auth is a middleware seam: replace localAuth with an OAuth verifier, nothing else changes.
The notes_jobs table is the cache: one generation serves every user and playlist.

recall.q: Why add a Node backend instead of extending the Python server?
recall.a: Python is a heavy, slow-job worker with in-memory jobs. Users, playlists and progress need a durable DB and an auth seam, which Express + SQLite does simply, and Node gives one front door that proxies the AI work.

sections.title: playlist import flow
sections.subtitle: paste a link, get a local copy

items: `importpl.js` extracts the `list=` id (10-64 chars) and asks aq-api: `GET /api/v1/import/youtube?url=`.
Node re-checks the id and forwards only a canonical playlist URL; Python validates again, then yt-dlp lists entries.
Server returns {id, title, channel, count, videos[], truncated, skipped}; private/deleted videos are skipped.
`cleanResponse` re-validates every field; the dialog previews title, count, total time, thumbnails.
`uniqueName` suggests "Title (2)" when the name is taken.
`store.createWithVideos(name, desc, videos, source)` writes once, with `source: {type: youtube, listId, url, importedAt}`.

blocks.text: Nothing syncs back to YouTube. The imported playlist is a copy; you can still add your own videos.

diagram.title: import
diagram.caption: link in, playlist out

key_takeaways: Validation happens twice: in the browser for UX, in Python for safety.
Limits: 200 videos per import, 2 playlist fetches at once, own rate bucket.
The response is treated as untrusted and re-sanitised by cleanResponse.

recall.q: Why re-validate the playlist response in the UI when the server already did?
recall.a: Defence in depth: the UI never trusts network data. cleanResponse drops bad ids, trims long text and caps the list, so a compromised or buggy server cannot inject markup or oversized data.

sections.title: progress calculation
sections.subtitle: time-based, not count-based

blocks.text: Progress is **watched seconds divided by total seconds**, so one 3-hour lecture weighs more than ten 2-minute clips. It is computed on the fly by `sumVideos` in `store.js`; nothing stores a percentage.
pct = round(100 * watchedSec / totalSec) (done video counts its full duration)

items: Each unique video is counted once, even if it sits in several playlists.
Per video: `watchInfo` -> state new / partial / done; done = ended or >= 95%.
Cap rules: never 100% while seconds are missing; never 0% once something was watched.
No known durations at all: fall back to finished videos / total videos.
`progressTime` renders "14 of 36 min" or "1 hr 2 min of 4 hr 30 min+" (+ means some durations unknown).

blocks.title: worked example
blocks.text: Playlist of 3 videos: 10:00 (done), 20:00 (watched 5:00), 30:00 (new). watched = 600 + 300 = 900 s, total = 3600 s, pct = 25%, done = 1 of 3.

diagram.title: progress pipeline
diagram.caption: from player seconds to the bar on a card

key_takeaways: Percent is derived each time from seconds; it is never stored.
Duplicates across playlists are counted once, in `overall()` too.
Edge rules prevent a misleading 0% or 100%.

recall.q: Why weight progress by time instead of counting finished videos?
recall.a: Videos differ wildly in length; counting them makes a 2-minute clip equal to a 3-hour lecture. Seconds watched over total seconds matches what the user feels, with a video-count fallback when durations are unknown.

sections.title: security
sections.subtitle: defence in layers

rows: Python and Node both bind 127.0.0.1 only; never 0.0.0.0
DNS-rebinding guard: only localhost names; POST and `/api/playlist` need a local Origin
key regex, model regex, 2048-char URL cap, 64 KB body cap, 11-char video ids
API keys live in memory for one job; `_redact` scrubs logs and errors; never returned by the API
CSP per route, nosniff, frame options, no-referrer, same-origin resource policy
notes.html allowed only its own inline scripts by SHA-256 hash; framed only by local pages
textContent only (no innerHTML); player embed from validated ids on youtube-nocookie.com
job id = 32 hex chars, path stays inside `output/`; all SQL parameterised and scoped by user_id

blocks.text: Known gap: login is not built yet. aq-api runs everything as the built-in local user (id 1); its `authenticate` seam is where OAuth goes. A key saved with Remember is plain text in localStorage.

diagram.title: layers a request crosses
diagram.caption: outermost first

key_takeaways: Local-only by default: bind, host check, origin check.
Never trust input (regex, caps) and never echo secrets (redaction).
Generated HTML is sandboxed by a hash-based CSP and framing rules.

recall.q: How do you stop a malicious web page from using your local notes server?
recall.a: The server answers only localhost Host headers (blocks DNS rebinding) and rejects any POST or playlist request whose Origin is not a local page. CORS allows the same set only, so another site's browser requests are refused.

sections.title: run & deploy
sections.subtitle: three commands, three ports

items: `start.ps1` creates `.venv`, installs `.[web]` only when pyproject.toml changed, opens the browser.
Copy `backend\.env.example` to `backend\.env` and add a Groq or Gemini key (or paste one in the UI).
`npm start` in aq-api opens `data/aq.db`, applies `sql/` migrations and serves the UI (`PORT`, `DB_FILE`, `PY_NOTES_URL` override defaults).
Open http://127.0.0.1:5180/ - never double-click index.html (a file:// page sends `Origin: null`, which is rejected).

blocks.code:

blocks.text: Config: `LNA_PORT` changes the worker port; `LNAI_BROWSER` picks Edge/Chrome; `FFMPEG_PATH` points to ffmpeg for Whisper.

diagram.title: boot sequence
diagram.caption: worker first, then the API that depends on it

key_takeaways: Two processes to run: the Python worker (:5055) and aq-api (:5180).
Everything binds to 127.0.0.1; this is a local app, not yet a hosted deployment.
Edge or Chrome must be installed to get PDFs; ffmpeg only for caption-less videos.

recall.q: What would you change to deploy this beyond a laptop?
recall.a: Put aq-api behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS and real OAuth, move SQLite to a managed DB if multi-instance, run the Python worker with a production WSGI server and a real queue, and keep the worker on a private network.

sections.title: tests & quality
sections.subtitle: everything mocked, nothing live

rows: URL parsing, caption cleaning, fallback chain, Whisper chunks
JSON repair, retries, pacing, map-reduce, validation
playlist id parsing, entry cleaning, limits
fixture notes and raw LLM output
playlists, progress, notes, security (node --test, in-memory DB)

blocks.text: Run `python -m pytest` from `lecture-notes-ai` (`pip install -e ".[web,dev]"`). `LNA_OFFLINE=1` skips the one live-network test. aq-api: `npm test` (`node --test`, in-memory SQLite, fake Python via injected `fetchImpl`).
Because all provider and YouTube calls are mocked, the suite is fast and free, so it can run on every change.

diagram.title: test pyramid
diagram.caption: unit tests per engine module, one API suite on top

key_takeaways: About 185 Python cases plus 32 aq-api tests; no network or API keys needed.
The server's `load_modules` is monkeypatchable, which is how test_api isolates the engine.
One optional live test is behind LNA_OFFLINE.

recall.q: How do you test code that calls YouTube and paid LLMs?
recall.a: Mock the boundaries: HTTP responses for providers and fake transcripts for ingest, with fixtures like sample_llm_output.json. Tests then assert parsing, retries, validation and rendering without network or keys.

sections.title: limits & future scope
sections.subtitle: what is missing, in order

items: **Limits today**: YouTube only; private, age-restricted and live videos fail; caption-less videos need a Groq key + ffmpeg; PDFs need Edge/Chrome; very long lectures take minutes and hit free-tier rate limits.
**Auth**: no login yet. Add OAuth in aq-api's middleware; make every playlist/progress row user-scoped.
**Sync**: today write-through with a dirty flag and last-writer-wins progress; next is per-user data and smarter multi-device conflict handling.
**Queue**: replace threads + memory jobs with a persistent queue so restarts keep jobs.
**Deploy**: HTTPS, reverse proxy, production WSGI server, hosted DB.
**Product**: notes search, per-video notes tab in the player, spaced-repetition from recall questions, more sources than YouTube.

blocks.text: Everything on this list fits the existing seams: the auth middleware, the notes cache by video_id and the stateless worker.

diagram.title: roadmap
diagram.caption: earliest to latest

key_takeaways: The seams (auth middleware, video_id cache, stateless worker) are already in place.
Order matters: auth before multi-device, queue before hosting.
Biggest user-visible wins: login, notes search, revision from recall questions.

recall.q: If you had one more sprint, what would you build first?
recall.a: Authentication in aq-api, because every other feature (per-user playlists, multi-device progress, hosted deploy) needs real user identity first, and the middleware seam already exists.

glossary.definition: The Node/Express + SQLite application backend: users, playlists, progress, notes records; serves the UI on :5180.
The Python Flask service on :5055 that makes transcripts, notes and PDFs; stateless about users.
The pip-installable Python package behind the CLI, the library and the web server.
One notes generation run in the worker, tracked in memory with stage and percent.
The validated structure (meta, cover, sections, glossary, recap) that the renderer draws.
Cleaned, timed caption segments of a video, the only input the LLM sees.
Long-lecture strategy: digest each slice, compose sections in batches, then write cover and recap.
Speech-to-text (Groq whisper-large-v3-turbo) used only when a video has no captions.
Server-side request forgery: tricking the server into fetching internal URLs; blocked by strict video-id parsing.
Content-Security-Policy header deciding which scripts, frames and styles a page may use.
Attack making a web page reach localhost services; stopped by only answering local Host names.
First-Last-Invert-Play animation technique used by split.js to morph the list into a nav.
Immediately-invoked function expression; each UI file wraps itself in one and exports onto window.AQ.
Playlist card: greyscale cover that reveals colour under a pointer spotlight.
Per-video {pos, dur, done, updated} stored under aq.watch.v1.
Reopening a video at its saved position; button label becomes Resume m:ss.
The 11-character YouTube id; primary key for notes cache and watch progress.
Planned login method; will plug into aq-api's auth middleware.
Client-side throttle that keeps LLM calls under the provider's tokens-per-minute limit.
The yellow Q/A box ending each notebook page, written as an interview question.

recap.title: the whole picture, recapped
points: UI (vanilla JS) shows playlists, plays videos, tracks progress; it talks to one door, aq-api on :5180.
aq-api (Node, Express, SQLite) owns users, playlists, progress and the notes cache by video_id.
The Python worker (:5055) turns a video id into notes: ingest -> llm -> validate -> pdf.
Notes generation is a job: start, poll stage/percent, then view notes.html or download the PDF.
Progress is time-based: watched seconds over total seconds, derived on the fly.
Security is layered: localhost bind, host/origin guard, input caps, redaction, CSP.
Seams for the future: auth middleware, notes cache, stateless worker.
